themes.theme: Ban on Letting Agent Fees - Core Policy
themes.reason: States that primary legislation will be used to implement the ban, but this is a brief statement of intent rather than detail on how delivery will work; the implementation case does not hinge on this alone.
Concerns a related but separate policy question (deposit size/affordability) rather than how the fee ban itself will be rolled out, so it does not carry the implementation argument.
Defines scope of permissible charges (what counts as a fee vs legitimate holding deposit) rather than the mechanics of delivering and enforcing the ban.
Clarifies which charges remain allowed, a scoping/definition matter rather than a description of the implementation method or enforcement approach.
Addresses a specific practice to be prohibited within the ban's scope, not how the ban will be rolled out or enforced.
Bears on a side-effect risk of the ban (discrimination) rather than on the chosen implementation or enforcement method itself.

This is the central pillar of the implementation argument, explaining who will enforce the ban (local authorities/Trading Standards), the option of a lead enforcement authority, and comparison to the Estate Agent sector model as precedent and alternative-method discussion.
Presents tenant awareness and challenge as a key mechanism for enforcing the ban, explicitly described as a tool to reduce burden on authorities, making it one of the chosen delivery methods.
Offers a supplementary enforcement-support idea (better data sharing) that strengthens but is not essential to the core enforcement architecture already established.
Discusses wider, still-undecided regulatory options as additional measures being explored, functioning as a secondary consideration rather than the chosen implementation route.
Directly addresses how non-compliance will be penalised (civil vs criminal, fine levels, banning orders), which is essential to explaining how the ban will actually be enforced in practice.
